body:
Today's scan turned up zero arbitrage opportunities across the 79 live contracts tracked on Kalshi and Polymarket — a quiet day, not a broken scanner. Both venues' order books are pricing gold consistently with each other: Kalshi's September 30, 2026 settle above $4,330.99 contract sits near a coin-flip (bid 0.58 / ask 0.64), and Polymarket's touch $4,450 this week contract is priced similarly (0.58/0.65), which lines up with where spot has actually been trading. News coverage this week put gold around $4,382.51 to $4,443.20 per ounce over the last 24 hours, and a separate report had it at $4,371 per ounce as of 9 a.m. Eastern on September 4, 2026. So the strike ladders on both platforms (Kalshi runs from $3,850 to $5,500; Polymarket's touch contracts cluster near $4,000–$4,550) aren't arbitrary — they're bracketing the actual market.

The bigger story is the level itself: gold has had an extraordinary run. One recap noted prices have surged to record highs, up over 25% since early 2025, driven by inflation and uncertainty, and Forbes flagged an all-time high of $5,597.23 on January 29, 2026. That backdrop explains why both platforms' most actively traded strikes now sit in the $4,300–$4,700 zone rather than the $2,600 range that was record territory just two years ago.

Mechanically, a reminder for readers: Kalshi's contracts here are settle markets, resolving on a single official price at a fixed future date (e.g., 5:00 PM EDT, Sept 30, 2026), while Polymarket's are touch markets, paying out if gold crosses a level at any point during the window. That structural difference — not mispricing — is usually why similarly-labeled contracts on the two platforms carry different odds, and it's the most common reason an apparent cross-platform edge turns out to be comparing two different bets rather than free money.
headline: No arbitrage found across 79 gold contracts as Kalshi and Polymarket price consistently with spot
